source: Crichton, Agrawala, Hanrahan (2021) The Role of Working Memory in Program Tracing
finding: Four small lab experiments on holding variable/value pairs in memory while tracing code. People held about 7 pairs in pure memorization. Adding mental arithmetic did not reliably cut capacity.
numbers: Exp1 N=15: recall 6.5 (SD 3.7) pairs for letter names, 7.2 (SD 3.4) for noun names; Wilcoxon p=0.45, no name effect. Exp2 N=14 (1 excluded): fewer pairs than Exp1 but not significant; over half of errors were substitution (swapped bindings), 70% more substitution than calculation errors. Exp3 N=12 (3 dropped): 9 of 12 kept one strategy at least 70% of the time (linear vs on-demand). Exp4 N=14: mostly linear tracing; inner-vs-leaf revisit prediction from working memory theory not supported.
limits: No expert vs novice contrast, no chunking manipulation; synthetic straight-line code; N 12 to 15 per experiment; between-experiment comparison.
agent_relevance: Capacity of about 7 bindings is a human number, not a model one. Failure is binding swaps. Suggests the schema should externalize state (a written variable table) rather than rely on memory.

source: Ikutani et al. (2021) Expert Programmers Have Fine-Tuned Cortical Representations of Source Code (eNeuro)
finding: fMRI decoding of the functional category of code snippets. Skill on a 10 second code-categorization task rose with competitive-programming rating, and decoding accuracy in seven frontal, parietal and temporal regions tracked skill.
numbers: N=30 (expert, middle, novice; AtCoder rating mean 954, SD 865, n=20 rated). Categorization accuracy 76.0% (SD 13.5) correlated with rating r=0.593 p=0.0059 (n=20); r=0.722 p=0.000007 with novices as zero (n=30). Subcategory task r=0.688 (n=20), r=0.735 (n=30).
limits: Cross-sectional; recognition of what a snippet does, not recall of scrambled code; no direct chunk-size measure; 10 s viewing; competitive-programming expertise only.
agent_relevance: Expertise looks like fast retrieval of function category from code. Closest neural support for a recognition/chunk account; favors an operator that labels code by purpose first.

source: Kuo and Prat (2024) Computer programmers show distinct, expertise-dependent brain responses to violations in form and meaning (Sci Rep)
finding: EEG while reading Python lines. Expertise sharpened the brain response to syntax violations (P600) but not to semantic implausibility (N400).
numbers: N=45 analysed (62 recruited, 16 lost to artifacts); split at 75% on a 72-item Python test: 27 experts, 18 novices (visualisation only; analysis continuous). Behaviour: expertise x syntax acceptance b=22.81 p<0.001; semantic x expertise b=-5.30 p=0.051. P600 syntax effect b=2.97 p<0.001; expertise x syntax P600 b=1.04 p<0.001; N400 interaction b=0.45 p=0.025; no expertise x semantic ERP effect.
limits: Students with at least one quarter of Python, so narrow expertise range; only for-loops and list comprehensions; cross-sectional; paper does not discuss chunking.
agent_relevance: Expertise shows up first as automatic rule knowledge (form), not deeper meaning sensitivity. A cheap syntax check is worth running before spending reasoning on meaning.

source: Liu and Bedny (2025) Learning to Program Recycles Preexisting Frontoparietal Population Codes of Logical Algorithms (J Neurosci)
finding: No clear new neural codes after one semester of Python. For-versus-if algorithm structure was already decodable from pseudocode before the course and the same code was reused for Python.
numbers: N=22 novices scanned before and after one Python semester. 'For' vs 'if' decodable in intraparietal sulcus and prefrontal cortex pre and post; control auditory cortex at chance; authors state they found no clear evidence of representational change; one control result 54.9% p=0.04 possibly false positive.
limits: Beginner-level code only, N=22, pseudocode pre vs code post is indirect, no expert group.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to a story where expertise means building new chunk representations early; learning may reuse general logic codes. Chunk gains may need far more practice than a semester.

source: Wyrich, Bogner, Wagner (2023) 40 Years of Designing Code Comprehension Experiments: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Mapping of 95 code-comprehension experiments, 1979 to 2019. Samples are mostly students, and few studies link snippets to comprehension theory such as beacons or chunking.
numbers: 95 studies; 53.7% all-student samples, 9.5% all-professional, 24.2% students plus professionals, 7.4% students plus faculty. Nine studies removed beacons and obfuscated names to force line-by-line bottom-up reading. Authors name chunking, plans and beacons as 1980s theories with very few newer ones.
quote: chunking of parts of the code to higher-level abstractions
limits: Mapping study: no pooled effect sizes, so it cannot say whether the expertise effect holds up in size.
agent_relevance: Warns that expert claims rest on thin samples with different expertise definitions. Treat 'experts chunk' as a design hypothesis, not a measured law.

source: Kou et al. (2024) Do Large Language Models Pay Similar Attention Like Human Programmers When Generating Code? (FSE)
finding: Six LLMs including GPT-4 attend to different parts of a task description than programmers do. About a quarter of wrong code could be traced to five attention patterns.
numbers: 6 LLMs, 2 benchmarks; two coders labeled important words (7 of 29.6 words per prompt agreed; property keywords 45.2%). 211 incorrect snippets (172 CodeGen-2.7B, 39 GPT-4): 57 (27%) explained by attention patterns. Perturbation-based attention preferred in a user study of 22 programmers. Alignment F1 about 45 to 52% at top-10.
limits: Looks at the task description, not code chunks; programmer labels from two authors; attention from older open models.
agent_relevance: Models miss operation and data-type words that humans mark as key. A first step that lists key operations and data types of the task, checked by code, targets a measured gap.

source: Li et al. (2024) Do Machines and Humans Focus on Similar Code? Explainability of LLMs in Code Summarization
finding: Negative result. SHAP-based model focus did not line up with human eye-tracking focus on Java code, and alignment did not predict summary quality.
numbers: 68 Java methods; per method a Spearman correlation between human fixation and model focus was significant (p<=0.05) for at most 22% of methods. Baseline: significant for 100% of methods between human duration and fixation count, and 85% between two models. Mean rho small among the significant ones. No significant relation between alignment and summary quality.
limits: Small stimulus set; SHAP is one proxy for model focus; no expert/novice split as main analysis.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model reads code the way an expert does. Any 'expert reading order' scaffold must be tested on the model, not borrowed from human data.

source: Hooda et al. (2025) Do Large Code Models Understand Programming Concepts? Counterfactual Analysis for Code Predicates
finding: Ten code models lose accuracy when programs are mutated in ways that break data flow. This is a machine version of the scrambled-program test.
numbers: 10 models; mutations: variable rename, if-else flip, def-use break, independent swap. Average modification effect as high as 34%; some mutations made over 20% of tasks fail; independent-swap (order-insensitive) is best understood. Def-use break only 22 valid problems in HumanEval/MBPP.
limits: Code completion on 75% prefixes of HumanEval and MBPP, so contamination possible; not an expert-novice comparison.
agent_relevance: Models depend on surface form and variable names. Gives a ready test: mutate or rename and see if the scaffold's answer survives (guardrail G3).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) cAST: Enhancing Code RAG with Structural Chunking via Abstract Syntax Tree
finding: Cutting code into chunks along syntax-tree boundaries beat fixed-line chunks for retrieval-augmented code generation.
numbers: Recall@5 +4.3 points on RepoEval; Pass@1 +2.67 points on SWE-bench Lite (300 problems); StarCoder2-7B average +5.5 points on RepoEval; up to +4.3 on CrossCodeEval. Doubling context length did not reliably help; shorter context lowered scores from chunk truncation. Max chunk size sweep 1000 to 3000 gave nDCG 68.4 to 72.3.
limits: Chunking here means retrieval units, not human memory chunks; gains are a few points; fixed 4000 token budget.
agent_relevance: Closest working AI use of meaningful-unit chunking. Whole-function units beat line splits, matching the human finding that experts recall intact meaningful units.

source: Issever, Catalbas, Duran (2023) Examining Factors Influencing Cognitive Load of Computer Programmers (Brain Sci)
finding: Reanalysis of the public EMIP eye-tracking data. Age and native-language distance weighed more on cognitive-load proxies than programming years.
numbers: N=216 programmers, 2 Java tasks. Canonical correlation r=0.581 p<0.001. Share of influence: age 18.0%, linguistic distance 15.4%, gender 0.255%. Years of programming correlated with task duration r=0.330; experience in the task language r=0.404 (both p<0.001); age with pupil-radius SD r=0.318.
limits: Secondary analysis; two OO tasks; no chunking measure; load inferred from eye signals.
agent_relevance: Moderators are many and large. Experience is one weak predictor among several, so a single expert-vs-novice mode is too crude for an agent prompt.

source: Shneiderman (1976) Exploratory experiments in programmer behavior
finding: Founding result as commonly cited: experienced programmers recalled intact short programs better than scrambled-line versions. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact N and recall rates not verified here.
limits: Recalled from the literature; Fortran-era; low confidence on details.
agent_relevance: Origin of the scrambled-program test. Hooda et al. (b08) is its LLM analogue.

source: McKeithen, Reitman, Rueter, Hirtle (1981) Knowledge organization and skill differences in computer programmers
finding: Expert, intermediate and novice programmers recalled ALGOL W keywords; experts clustered by meaning and showed the advantage for real programs, not random ones. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact N and recall rates not verified here.
limits: Small groups; one language; recall of keywords; low confidence on details.
agent_relevance: Supports expertise as organization, not capacity. The agent should group facts by role, not by reading order.

source: Adelson (1981, 1984) Problem solving and the development of abstract categories in programming languages / When novices surpass experts
finding: Experts group code by abstract function; novices by surface syntax. The 1984 follow-up showed the pattern depends on task framing. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact numbers not verified here.
limits: Task framing changes which grouping appears: boundary condition on the chunk story.
agent_relevance: Depth of grouping depends on the task; label by purpose first, by syntax second.

source: Wiedenbeck (1986) Beacons in computer program comprehension
finding: Experts spotted key lines (beacons) more reliably than novices when they were present. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact N and accuracy not verified here.
limits: Beacons need conventional code; obfuscated names remove the cue (Wyrich et al. note nine studies strip beacons).
agent_relevance: Beacons are surface cues that can mislead; guard with checks (G3).

source: Gilmore and Green (1984) Programming plans and programming expertise
finding: Boundary condition: the expert advantage depended on whether the notation made the plan visible. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact numbers not verified here.
limits: Notation dependent; small N; low confidence on details.
agent_relevance: Presentation format can erase or create an expertise effect. Present code in a format that exposes structure.

source: Barfield (1986) Expert-novice differences for software: implications for problem-solving and knowledge acquisition
finding: Extension of recall-based studies; reported experts chunk program text into larger meaningful pieces. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact numbers not verified here.
limits: From memory; low confidence on details.
agent_relevance: Supporting but not independent proof.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis (IJMMS)
finding: Source of the hypothesis: expert debuggers used a system view and breadth-first search; novices went depth-first. Stated as propositions to test. Not reread this session.
numbers: Sample size and rates not verified here.
limits: Small protocol study; author calls findings propositions.
agent_relevance: Breadth-first system view before depth is the scaffold-relevant claim. It stays a hypothesis; test it on the agent directly.

source: Chase and Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Origin of the chunk account: masters recall real positions far better than random ones. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact figures not verified here.
limits: Later work found some master advantage on random boards too.
agent_relevance: Source of the scrambled-input test design.

source: Gobet and Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill
finding: Challenge to a pure chunk story: masters still beat novices on random positions, which fits larger templates. Not reread this session.
numbers: Exact numbers not verified here.
limits: Chess, not code; random positions can contain accidental meaningful pieces.
agent_relevance: A residual expert advantage on scrambled input does not refute chunking, and a drop does not prove it.

source: Busjahn et al. (2015) Eye Movements in Code Reading: Relaxing the Linear Order (ICPC)
finding: Commonly cited: novices read code more linearly than experts. Seen only in a Crossref list (153 citations); content not read.
numbers: Group sizes and linearity values not verified here.
limits: Small groups; short snippets; not read.
agent_relevance: Human experts do not read in file order. A model reading strictly top to bottom may use the novice strategy.

source: Peitek, Siegmund, Apel (2020) What Drives the Reading Order of Programmers? An Eye Tracking Study (ICPC)
finding: Follow-up on reading order; page blocked (HTTP 403), contents not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Contents not seen.
agent_relevance: Open item: is reading order an expertise effect or a code-layout effect.

source: Bauer, Siegmund et al. (2019) Indentation: Simply a Matter of Style or Support for Program Comprehension? (ICPC)
finding: Believed to be a replication of Miara et al. (1983) indentation benefit, reported not to confirm a clear benefit. Only title and metadata seen; details not verified.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Contents not seen; recalled from memory.
agent_relevance: Example of a classic 1980s programmer-behavior effect that may not replicate cleanly; reason to distrust old small-N results.

source: Fucci et al. (2019) A Replication Study on Code Comprehension and Expertise using Lightweight Biometric Sensors (ICPC)
finding: Replication on code comprehension and expertise with biometric sensors. Only title and metadata seen; results not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Contents not seen.
agent_relevance: Open item to read next for the replication outcome.

source: Castel et al. (2003) Experts sometimes show more false recall than novices: a cost of knowing too much
finding: Boundary condition outside programming: expert schemas can raise false recall of plausible but absent items. Only title seen in Crossref; details not verified.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not programming; contents not seen.
agent_relevance: Chunk-based expectations cause confident wrong fills. Matches an agent completing familiar code patterns wrongly; supports held-out checks.

source: Gobet et al. (2001) Chunking mechanisms in human learning (Trends Cogn Sci)
finding: Review arguing chunk models need links between chunks (templates), a rival to a fixed count of independent chunks. Not reread this session.
numbers: Not verified here.
limits: Recalled from the literature; domain is mostly chess.
agent_relevance: Rival accounts (template, long-term working memory) predict different scrambled-input results; matters when designing a test of the breadth-first hypothesis.
